newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Southern Africa bourses seen worth $400 bln by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Southern Africa bourses seen worth $400 bln by 2000.

text.p: The market capitalisation of Southern Africa's stock exchanges is set to leap by 60 percent to $400 billion by the turn of the century, U.S. securities house Merrill Lynch predicted on Thursday.

"We believe conservatively that by the year 2000 the market capitalisation of Southern Africa will approach $400 billion which is equal to that of Latin America today," Brian Henderson, senior vice-president, told an investment conference.

Henderson noted that the market capitalisation of the region's bourses had already more than doubled from $105 billion in 1992 to $250 billion at the end of 1996, and said the trend would continue as businesses increasingly tapped equity markets.
At the same time there was a growing interest in overseas markets among U.S. investors whose attention was finally turning to Africa, he said. South Africa still dominates the region's
six other established bourses in Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, Mauritius and Swaziland, accounting for 97 percent of the market capitalisation.
But more and more listings are being seen in regional markets, while new exchanges are springing up.
Malawi's stock exchange opened its doors for business earlier this year, while Tanzania will launch later in 1997 and Mozambique has a project in hand to establish a bourse.

Maria Ramos, director general of finance in South Africa, told the same meeting that the flow of funds into emerging markets could be a boon to local capital markets. But government and banks in Southern Africa had to pay more attention to managing the attendant risks.
"Our financial institutions need to look at risk management more closely because financial institutions under stress, particularly in smaller economies, create intolerable systemic risk," she said.
